content.text: # Code Review Rules Earlier this session you loaded the spacing, typography, color and accessibility principles. Check the build against these first. The visual design, accessibility and content rules are ordered first below. ## Match the requested change Classify the request as repair, polish, or redesign: restore behavior, refine layout, or rebuild layout and components. Follow the user's scope, not analytics-only tool context. Do not downgrade redesign to polish, expand repair, or turn token export/source inspection into a redesign. Keep the selected design system and assigned icon family/variant unless the user requests a change. Use exact returned icon names/source, never substitute packs, emoji, or invented SVGs. Inventory sections, components, states and responsive layouts; map requested patterns to real system components and record missing primitives. Plan structural changes and component adoption before redesigning. Rebuild the requested hierarchy, layout and interactions; token swaps and unused imports do not count. Preserve unrelated behavior, accessibility and production/control boundaries. Preserve all supplied paragraphs, reviews, offer details, links and disclosures, including collapsed answers and inactive tabs, unless the user requests cuts or rewrites. Require a source-to-render content comparison; investigate every omission, not just section counts. A shortened fixture is not a completed page. Label partial prototypes and never treat their checks as full-page evidence. Compare before/after renders of the same content and states at the same desktop and mobile widths. Show which planned structural changes and component adoption are visible; verify the selected icons, spacing, hierarchy, and working interactions. Copy and accessibility fixes alone do not complete a redesign. Tool calls, generated files, or a source-only review are not visual evidence. If a baseline or rendered check is unavailable, name the missing evidence and report the redesign as unverified. Keep all existing build, accessibility, hover, comprehension, and review gates. ## Explain design trade-offs Before choosing or changing a design direction, tell the user what each real option gains and loses, which users or team bear the cost, and why you recommend it for this project's known audience, goals, and constraints. Use a short line per option: "Gain: ...; lose: ...; affects: ...; fits because: ...". Load get-ux-principle with topic "tradeoffs" when deeper guidance is needed. Use the current conversation and project evidence. Label assumptions and predicted effects. Do not invent research, conversion gains, metrics, or project facts. If the user has already chosen, explain the accepted trade-off without reopening the choice. Keep minor edits brief; this adds no approval step and never excuses an accessibility or safety failure. Put the explanation in the conversation or requested project handoff, not extra product UI copy. Before presenting the result, check that material gains and losses were communicated and report any changed trade-off. ## Before you present this screen These rules were read against source. They cannot see layout. Four checks remain: 1. Dashboard review: call `review-dashboard-structure` with the complete source, unchanged request fixture, factual interpretation, and installed component source. FAIL blocks completion. Use it to compare the h1 and supporting line to the request and enforce title, metrics, records, interpretation order. The header has one primary action; metric values lead labels; action/selection color differs from status color. Use installed semantic variants. Do not invent trends. The overview is not a workflow step. When a fixture lists the overview first, exclude it from progress; with three remaining task screens use no stepper. An active nav label is not the page title. 2. Call `inspect-spacing` on the rendered DOM at 1440, 1728 and 390 wide. The first call returns a capture script and measures nothing; the layout is measured only when a second call, with the captured states, returns status `completed`. Rules read code; only measurement catches a label sitting 9px off its own circle, an active state that is 2px wider than its siblings and shifts the row, or a sidebar that leaves page background beside it on a wide screen. A Shopify theme preview or a React Native web export is a rendered DOM, so measure it. A native SwiftUI or Android app has no DOM: review a simulator screenshot at each screen size against these rules instead, and say that spacing was not measured. 3. Call `check-comprehension` on the screen's visible copy, and fix every finding it returns. 4. For dashboards, deploy the exact source to a public HTTPS preview, then call `finalize-dashboard-review` with that URL, the exact complete and visible source, unchanged fixture, and installed component source. Better Design's own browser captures the preview at 390, 1440, and 1728, content-addresses the live deployment, derives the factual interpretation, and issues the only valid review receipt. No trusted browser capture means incomplete. An invalid deployment revision, invalid geometry, or hidden fixture field also blocks approval. Any later source or deployment edit voids the receipt. Then confirm every nav item, link, tab and button works. ## Presentations A deck passes only on rendered evidence. For every slide: 1. Call `check-comprehension` with `surface: "slide"`. Keep one idea per slide and fix every density finding. 2. Render the deck and review a screenshot of every slide: the title reads first, one element holds the eye, and nothing competes with it. Text checks and `inspect-spacing` cannot see this, so no score stands in for the screenshot. ## Check the rules below in two passes An agent that reviews its own screen in one pass tends to approve it. Split the review: 1. Per rule: give each rule section below (each `# ` heading) to its own subagent, in a clean context that holds only that section and the source. A host without subagents checks one section at a time and writes down its findings before it reads the next. 2. Skeptic pass: give every flag to one fresh subagent that tries to disprove it. It keeps a flag only when it can cite the file and line that break the rule. Cite the rule ID with every finding: the `rule/…` line under each rule heading. Read its Exceptions line before you flag. A surface listed under coverage gaps has no rule yet, so say that instead of inventing one. Fix every critical and serious finding before you present. # Accessibility (WCAG 2.1) ## Accessibility (WCAG 2.1) ### Critical Issues These issues MUST be fixed before shipping. They prevent users from accessing content. #### Images without alt text **ID:** `rule/image-needs-alt-text` **Source:** WCAG 2.1 SC 1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A) **Exceptions:** A purely decorative image takes an empty `alt=""`, which is the correct text alternative for it. **Rule:** All `` elements must have an `alt` attribute. ```tsx // ❌ Bad // ✅ Good // ✅ Good (decorative images) ``` **WCAG Reference:** 1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A) **Why it matters:** Screen readers cannot convey image content without alt text. Decorative images should use `alt=""` to indicate they should be skipped. #### Icon-only buttons missing aria-labels **ID:** `rule/icon-button-needs-name` **Source:** WCAG 2.1 SC 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A) **Exceptions:** A button with visible text inside takes its name from that text, so it needs no `aria-label`. **Rule:** Buttons without text content must have `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`. ```tsx // ❌ Bad // ✅ Good // ✅ Good (with visible text) ``` **WCAG Reference:** 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A) **Why it matters:** Screen reader users cannot understand button purpose without accessible names. #### Form inputs without labels **ID:** `rule/form-input-needs-label` **Source:** WCAG 2.1 SC 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions (Level A) **Exceptions:** An `` needs no label, because the user never sees or fills it. **Rule:** All ``, `
